method: Full1388-line pinned source read in contiguous1..600/601..1000/1001..1388 with Git/SHA256 verification. No AVX512 execution on ARM host.
findings: Hash-many decomposes inputs into16/8/4/1 groups with32-byte output per input; XOF-many uses same group widths but64-byte output blocks and always increments output-block counter. Distinct paths need distinct parity controls.

Four/eight lane counters use64-bit vector additions then low/high narrowing;16-lane counter uses low32 addition and top-bit carry detection with small offsets0..15. Wrap/carry logic requires actual runtime parity.

Vector transposition sizes4x4/8x8/16x16 words differ. Hash16 pads eight CV vectors with zero rows and stores lower256 bits of each transposed row; XOF16 transposes full16 vectors and stores512 bits. No output-overwrite bug inferred from shared helper.
storeu256/512 parameter annotations show dest16 but intrinsic writes32/64; call-site strides/contracts determine actual buffer requirement. Annotation mismatch is not independently proven overflow.

Compression paths read complete64-byte padded input even when logical block_len smaller. Caller contract must guarantee readable padding; full-block hash_many does not implement partial final-byte handling.

128/256-bit rotate intrinsics in AVX512 implementation still require AVX512VL-capable configuration, so vector width alone does not imply SSE/AVX2-safe fallback. Dispatcher gating previously reviewed separately.
Start/end flags apply first/last full block. Zero-input or zero-output-block loops do not write; nonzero counts require sufficient pointers/output capacity.

Prefetch uses+256 ahead and compile-time intrinsics/assembly alternatives are separate qualification gates. Source similarity to SSE/AVX2 and ARM parity does not establish AVX512 correctness or speed.
limits: No x86 hardware run, ABI/sanitizer qualification or throughput measurement; assembly variants remain unread.
